title: How beneficiaries get assigned to an MSSP ACO
questions: How are Medicare beneficiaries assigned to a Shared Savings Program ACO?
What are the two ways a patient becomes part of an MSSP ACO?
Explain MSSP beneficiary assignment at a high level
Does a patient have to enroll in an ACO to be attributed?
summary: Traditional Medicare beneficiaries never enroll in a Shared Savings Program ACO; CMS assigns them. There are two routes. First, voluntary alignment: a beneficiary who names an ACO professional as their primary clinician on Medicare.gov is prospectively assigned to that ACO, and that choice overrides claims. Second, claims-based assignment: CMS looks at where the beneficiary received the plurality of primary care services, measured in Medicare allowed charges, using a step-wise algorithm (a screening pre-step, Step 1 for primary care clinicians, Step 2 for certain specialists, and since PY2025 an expanded-window Step 3). Assignment is run separately for each benchmark and performance year, so a patient attributed one year may not be attributed the next. The ACO's certified participant list of billing TINs (plus CCNs for FQHCs, RHCs, Method II CAHs and ETA hospitals) defines which services count as 'inside' the ACO. The statutory basis is section 1899 of the Social Security Act, amended by the 21st Century Cures Act (adding FQHC/RHC services) and the Bipartisan Budget Act of 2018 (adding voluntary identification and a prospective assignment option).

title: Which beneficiaries are eligible for MSSP assignment
questions: Which Medicare beneficiaries can be assigned to an ACO?
Why are Medicare Advantage members excluded from MSSP assignment?
What eligibility screens does CMS apply before MSSP assignment?
summary: Before running the assignment algorithm, CMS screens beneficiaries for eligibility. For a benchmark or performance year a beneficiary needs at least one month of both Part A and Part B, cannot have any month of Part A-only or Part B-only coverage, cannot have any month of Medicare group (private) health plan enrollment such as Medicare Advantage, and must have lived in the US or its territories based on residence in the last month of the assignment window. Claims-based assignment additionally requires at least one primary care service from a physician who is an ACO professional in the ACO and is either a primary care physician or holds one of the listed specialty designations (an FQHC or RHC claim counts as a primary care physician service). Voluntarily aligned beneficiaries do not need a primary care visit at the ACO. Prospectively assigned beneficiaries are removed quarterly and at year end if they fail these exclusion criteria, and beneficiaries who died before the year starts are dropped. Beneficiaries who designate a primary clinician outside the ACO are excluded even if claims would assign them.

title: MSSP pre-step, Step 1, Step 2 and tie-breakers
questions: How does Step 1 of MSSP assignment work?
What is the difference between Step 1 and Step 2 in MSSP assignment?
Does MSSP attribution use visit counts or dollars?
How does CMS break ties in ACO assignment?
summary: MSSP claims-based assignment measures plurality in Medicare allowed charges (which include the beneficiary deductible) rather than visit counts; CMS notes dollars reduce the chance of ties. The pre-step identifies beneficiaries with at least one primary care service from an ACO physician who is a primary care physician or has an eligible specialty. Step 1 assigns the beneficiary to the ACO if primary care services from primary care physicians, nurse practitioners, physician assistants and clinical nurse specialists in the ACO exceed those from the same clinician types at any other ACO, non-ACO CCN, or non-ACO TIN. Step 2 applies only to beneficiaries with no primary care service from any PCP, NP, PA or CNS anywhere; it assigns based on the plurality of primary care services from eligible specialist physicians in the ACO. Ties go to the entity with the most recent primary care service from a primary care clinician, then the most recent from a Step-2 specialist, and finally random assignment. Services billed through a TIN that participates in more than one ACO are excluded from final assignment.

summary: The CY 2024 Physician Fee Schedule final rule added a third step to MSSP's step-wise assignment methodology, effective for performance years beginning January 1, 2025. Step 3 targets beneficiaries who would otherwise go unassigned because their recent primary care came from non-physician practitioners. It uses an expanded 24-month window (the normal 12-month assignment window plus the prior 12 months) and applies to beneficiaries who received primary care from nurse practitioners, physician assistants or clinical nurse specialists during the 12-month window and at least one primary care service from a physician used in assignment during the preceding 12 months. CMS also revised the definition of 'assignable beneficiary' to include people identified through the expanded window. CMS projected the change would add more than 760,000 assignable beneficiaries. NAACOS described it as expanding the lookback for a physician visit to two years starting in 2025.

title: Prospective vs preliminary prospective assignment with retrospective reconciliation
questions: What is the difference between prospective and retrospective assignment in MSSP?
How does preliminary prospective assignment with retrospective reconciliation work?
Which assignment window does prospective assignment use?
Can an ACO switch its assignment methodology?
summary: For agreement periods since July 1, 2019, BASIC and ENHANCED ACOs choose before the agreement period between two methods, and may change the election before any later performance year. Under preliminary prospective assignment with retrospective reconciliation, CMS gives a preliminary list at the start of the year, refreshes it quarterly on a rolling 12 months of claims, and determines final assignment using the calendar performance year itself, so the ACO is accountable for whoever turns out to have been treated there. Under prospective assignment, CMS fixes the list at the start of the year using an offset window (October through September before the year); a beneficiary on that list cannot be assigned to another ACO that year even if their care shifts, but is removed quarterly and at year end for exclusion criteria such as MA enrollment. The ACO remains accountable for prospectively assigned beneficiaries who die during the year. Voluntarily aligned beneficiaries are prospectively assigned under either method. Expenditures are always measured for the calendar performance year.

options: preliminary prospective assignment with retrospective reconciliation

title: MSSP voluntary alignment via Medicare.gov primary clinician designation
questions: What is voluntary alignment in the Shared Savings Program?
How does a patient choose their ACO through Medicare.gov?
Does voluntary alignment override claims-based attribution?

summary: Beneficiaries can log in to Medicare.gov (formerly MyMedicare.gov) and designate a 'primary clinician' they consider responsible for coordinating their overall care. If that clinician is an ACO professional in an MSSP ACO, the beneficiary is prospectively assigned to that ACO at the start of each benchmark and performance year, regardless of the ACO's track or chosen assignment method, and without needing a primary care visit there. The designation supersedes claims-based assignment, and naming a clinician outside any ACO removes the beneficiary from claims-based assignment. Alignment persists across years unless the beneficiary changes it, becomes ineligible, or the ACO terminates or changes its participant list. For 12-month performance years since 2020, CMS uses designations made through September 30 of the prior year (for PY2024, through September 30, 2023). Voluntary alignment was first used in PY2018. The CY 2025 rule broadened an exception so beneficiaries claims-assigned to certain condition-specific CMMI ACO models are handled consistently.

summary: An MSSP ACO is defined operationally by its certified ACO Participant List of Medicare-enrolled billing TINs, plus CCNs for FQHCs, RHCs, Method II critical access hospitals and electing-teaching-amendment hospitals sourced from PECOS. CMS uses this list to decide which primary care services were furnished 'in' the ACO for assignment, and also for the historical benchmark (the three years before the agreement), performance-year expenditures, the quality sample, SNF 3-day waiver eligibility and feedback reports. ACOs may add or remove participants annually, which re-runs assignment for benchmark years as well. If a participant TIN appears in more than one ACO, services billed through it are excluded when determining final assignment. Practically, attribution changes when practices join or leave, and an analyst reconstructing an ACO's population must use the participant list in force for that performance year. The CY 2026 rule requires mid-year participant list updates when a change of ownership creates a new TIN with no prior Medicare billing history.

title: ACO REACH claims-based alignment (PQEM services)
questions: How does claims-based alignment work in ACO REACH?
What is a PQEM service?
How does REACH alignment differ from MSSP assignment?
What lookback does REACH use for alignment?
summary: In ACO REACH, claims-based alignment compares weighted allowed charges for Primary Care Qualified Evaluation and Management (PQEM) services that a beneficiary received from each REACH ACO's participant providers against each non-participant billing TIN. It uses two alignment years: charges in the earlier year are weighted one-third and charges in the more recent year two-thirds, counting claims paid within three months after the second year. A two-track rule decides which clinicians count: if 10% or more of the beneficiary's PQEM allowed charges came from primary care specialists, alignment is based only on those clinicians; otherwise it is based on selected non-primary-care specialists. Ties go to the ACO whose participant billed the most recent PQEM service. A beneficiary must be alignment-eligible on January 1 and not already aligned to a program that takes precedence. Compared with MSSP, REACH uses a two-year weighted lookback rather than a single 12-month window, and claims alignment is always prospective.

title: ACO REACH voluntary alignment (SVA and MVA)
questions: How does voluntary alignment work in ACO REACH?
What is the difference between SVA and MVA?
When does a REACH voluntary alignment designation expire?
Can a voluntarily aligned REACH beneficiary be removed?
summary: ACO REACH supports two forms of voluntary alignment. Medicare.gov Voluntary Alignment (MVA) uses the beneficiary's primary clinician designation on Medicare.gov; Signed attestation-based Voluntary Alignment (SVA) uses a form (paper or electronic) in which the beneficiary names a participant provider as their main doctor or place of care. Either aligns the beneficiary regardless of claims. A designation is valid for a performance year if it was made no earlier than two years before the year starts, or if the designated provider billed a PQEM service for the beneficiary in the 24 months ending one month before the year. The most recent valid designation wins, and before the year starts voluntary alignment beats claims alignment. A beneficiary aligned only by voluntary alignment is dropped at settlement if they received no covered service from the ACO's participant or preferred providers during the year but did receive a PQEM service from an outside provider within the ACO's service area. Claims-aligned beneficiaries who also attest are treated as claims-aligned for benchmarking.

title: REACH alignment precedence and Prospective Plus

summary: CMS uses a cross-model governance process so a beneficiary is not aligned to more than one shared-savings initiative. For PY2024, the following took precedence over ACO REACH: the Maryland Primary Care Program, Kidney Care Choices, the Shared Savings Program (prospective assignment only), Primary Care First, the Vermont All-Payer ACO Model and Making Care Primary. Within REACH, ACOs can elect Prospective Plus alignment, which adds beneficiaries who voluntarily align (via MVA or SVA) at the start of each quarter (Q2 to Q4) during the performance year, provided they are eligible and not already aligned to a conflicting initiative. During these quarterly additions, a beneficiary already aligned to a REACH ACO is not removed or switched if they later attest to an outside provider. Claims-based alignment is mandatory and runs only before the year. These rules mean MSSP ACOs under retrospective reconciliation do not block REACH alignment, while prospectively assigned MSSP beneficiaries do.

title: Alignment for High Needs Population ACOs in REACH

summary: High Needs Population ACOs in ACO REACH serve Traditional Medicare beneficiaries with complex needs, including many dually eligible people, using a care model resembling PACE. They use the same claims-based and voluntary alignment mechanisms as other REACH ACOs, but a beneficiary must also meet High Needs eligibility criteria. CMS checks eligibility quarterly, so a beneficiary who would otherwise align has up to four chances per performance year; once found eligible they are aligned from the next quarter (January 1, April 1, July 1 or October 1) for the rest of the year. After alignment, the beneficiary is treated as High Needs eligible for the remaining performance years even if they stop meeting the clinical criteria, unless they lose general eligibility or are retrospectively removed; CMS describes this as protecting continuity of care and not penalizing ACOs for effective care. High Needs ACOs with more than 3,000 claims-aligned beneficiaries in a base year are benchmarked like Standard ACOs but keep High Needs risk adjustment.

title: How Medicare Advantage members enter value-based arrangements

summary: In Medicare Advantage, attribution starts with enrollment: the beneficiary chooses a private plan, and Medicare pays that plan a monthly risk-adjusted capitation. MedPAC reports MA covers 55 percent of eligible beneficiaries in 2025, with Medicare payments to plans of $494 billion in 2024. Plans then decide how to pay providers. Federal rules require MA coordinated care plans to offer each enrollee an ongoing source of primary care and to provide one to each enrollee who accepts, and to maintain a PCP network. Plans commonly tie members to a primary care provider or group and may delegate financial risk to that group through capitation or other incentive arrangements, subject to physician incentive plan rules. The specific mechanics of PCP selection, default assignment and delegation are set in plan and provider contracts rather than in a single federal methodology, so they vary by plan; no CMS public specification analogous to the MSSP assignment rules governs them.

title: MA capitation and delegated risk to physician groups (physician incentive plan rules)
questions: What rules govern capitation from Medicare Advantage plans to physician groups?
What is substantial financial risk in a physician incentive plan?
What is global capitation under MA rules?
Do MA plans have to provide stop-loss to capitated groups?
summary: When an MA organization pays physicians or groups through arrangements that could limit services, the physician incentive plan rules at 42 CFR 422.208 apply, including to intermediate entities such as IPAs. The regulation defines capitation as a fixed payment per patient per period covering a specified set of services regardless of volume, and global capitation as capitation covering both professional and institutional services. A group is at substantial financial risk when its risk for referral services (care it orders but does not furnish) exceeds a 25 percent threshold of potential payments; the rule applies to panels of 25,000 patients or fewer. Plans must ensure groups at substantial financial risk have stop-loss: aggregate coverage of 90 percent of referral costs above 25 percent of potential payments, or per-patient stop-loss covering at least 90 percent above deductibles set by panel size in CMS tables. Plans may never make specific payments to induce reducing medically necessary care for a particular enrollee.

title: Medicaid managed care enrollment: voluntary, mandatory, passive and default
questions: How do Medicaid beneficiaries get enrolled in a managed care plan?
What is passive enrollment in Medicaid managed care?
What happens if a Medicaid enrollee does not choose a plan?
Difference between voluntary and mandatory Medicaid managed care
summary: Under 42 CFR 438.54, states must run an enrollment system for each Medicaid managed care program. In voluntary programs, beneficiaries may choose managed care or stay in fee-for-service; the state either gives a choice period before enrollment or uses passive enrollment, placing the person in a plan while allowing them to keep it, switch plans, or opt for FFS. Without passive enrollment, someone who does not choose stays in FFS. In mandatory programs, beneficiaries must enroll in an MCO, PIHP, PAHP or PCCM; anyone who does not choose is placed by the state's default process (or stays in the passively assigned plan). States must send notices explaining the choices, the implications of not choosing, and the 90-day without-cause disenrollment period, and must give existing enrollees priority if a plan lacks capacity. KFF reports 78 percent of Medicaid enrollees (over 66 million people) were in comprehensive MCOs as of July 1, 2024, so auto-assignment drives a large share of Medicaid attribution.

title: Criteria states must use for Medicaid passive/default plan assignment

What factors can a state use in Medicaid passive enrollment?
summary: Federal rules constrain how states auto-assign Medicaid enrollees. A passive enrollment process may only assign to qualified plans, meaning plans not under an enrollment sanction and with capacity. It must try to preserve existing provider-beneficiary relationships (a provider who was a main source of Medicaid services in the prior year, identified from enrollment, FFS, encounter data or contact with the beneficiary) and relationships with providers that have traditionally served Medicaid. If that is not possible, the state must distribute beneficiaries equitably among plans without arbitrarily excluding any. States may layer in other criteria such as family members' plans, prior plan assignment, quality performance, procurement scores, and accessibility for people with disabilities. After a passive assignment, the state must notify the enrollee within 5 calendar days of the end of the choice window and explain the right to switch within 90 days. Because plan quality can be a factor, some states reward higher-performing MCOs with more default enrollment.

title: Attribution churn and leakage
questions: What is attribution churn in an ACO?
What is patient leakage and why does it matter for attribution?

summary: Attribution churn is the turnover of an ACO's attributed population between periods. In MSSP, CMS runs assignment separately for each benchmark and performance year, so a beneficiary assigned one year may not be assigned the next if their plurality of primary care shifts, they move to Medicare Advantage, die, or move abroad; quarterly preliminary lists under retrospective reconciliation can change every quarter. Participant list changes also reshuffle populations. Leakage refers to attributed patients receiving care outside the ACO's network. Leakage of primary care can flip attribution under plurality rules (or, in REACH, can trigger removal of a voluntarily aligned beneficiary who saw an outside PQEM provider in the service area and no ACO provider), while leakage of specialty or facility care leaves the ACO accountable for spending it does not control. Prospective assignment reduces mid-year churn because the list is locked except for exclusions, and voluntary alignment persists across years. These definitions are general concepts drawn from program rules rather than a single official definition.

title: MSSP minimum savings rate for one-sided ACOs

summary: The minimum savings rate (MSR) is a threshold, expressed as a percent of the updated benchmark, that an ACO's savings must meet or exceed before it can share in savings. CMS designed it to give confidence that measured savings reflect real efficiency rather than normal year-to-year variation, which is larger for small populations. One-sided BASIC Level A and B ACOs get a variable MSR based on assigned beneficiaries: 3.9 percent at 5,000 beneficiaries, falling to 3.0 percent at 10,000, 2.5 percent at 20,000, and 2.0 percent at 60,000 or more; values in between are interpolated (CMS's example: 5,333 beneficiaries gives 3.8 percent). Below 5,000 the MSR rises steeply, from 5.0 percent at 3,000 to 8.7 percent at 1,000 and 12.2 percent or more under 500. A separate exception lets certain low-revenue BASIC ACOs share savings below the MSR at half the normal rate for agreements starting 2024 or later.

The options are 0 percent; a fixed rate between 0.5 and 2 percent in 0.5 percent steps; or a variable rate that follows the one-sided size-based MSR table, with the MLR equal to the negative MSR. A higher threshold protects against small losses but also delays savings; a lower threshold does the reverse. If a two-sided ACO with a fixed MSR/MLR drops below 5,000 assigned beneficiaries in a performance year, CMS uses the variable size-based rate for that year and reverts afterwards.

title: How the MSSP historical benchmark is built
questions: How is an MSSP ACO's benchmark calculated?

summary: An MSSP ACO's benchmark is built from per capita Parts A and B FFS spending for beneficiaries who would have been assigned to it in the three benchmark years before the agreement period. CMS computes annualized, truncated per capita expenditures separately for four enrollment types (ESRD, disabled, aged/dual, aged/non-dual), trends benchmark years 1 and 2 to year-3 dollars using a blend of national and regional growth rates, risk-adjusts them, and weights the years 10, 30 and 60 percent in a first agreement period (equal weights when the benchmark is rebased for a renewing ACO). Adjustments are then added: the regional adjustment and, for 2024-onward agreements, a prior savings adjustment or (from 2025) a population/health-equity adjustment. Each performance year CMS 'updates' the benchmark for case-mix change and spending growth to produce the updated historical benchmark used at reconciliation, and 'adjusts' it for participant list or methodology changes. A new agreement period resets (rebases) the benchmark. Expenditures use a 3-month claims run-out with a completion factor.

summary: The regional adjustment moves an ACO's historical benchmark toward the risk-adjusted average spending of its regional service area (counties where its assigned beneficiaries live). A guardrail protects ACOs: if an ACO shows losses beyond its MLR (or negative MSR) under the three-way blend, CMS recomputes with the two-way blend and uses whichever yields smaller losses. title: Benchmark rebasing and the ratchet effect
questions: What is the ratchet effect in ACO benchmarks?
What does benchmark rebasing mean?
How has CMS tried to fix the MSSP ratchet effect?
summary: Rebasing resets an ACO's benchmark at the start of a new agreement period using its most recent spending. Because successful ACOs lower their own spending, rebasing can shrink the next benchmark, so savings today make future savings harder to earn; this is the 'ratchet effect.' Commenters on the CY 2024 rule raised it, noting early renewal triggers rebasing. A related ratchet arises when ACO savings drag down the national and regional trends used to update benchmarks. CMS has layered fixes: renewing ACOs' benchmark years are weighted equally rather than 10/30/60; the prior savings adjustment adds back up to 50 percent of recent savings (capped at 5 percent of national spending); the ACPT makes one-third of the annual update prospective; the regional adjustment blends toward regional spending; and the negative regional adjustment was effectively eliminated for 2024-onward agreements. CMS has also solicited comment on refining ACPT further to mitigate ratchet effects. LEAD, the REACH successor starting 2027, promises a predictable window without rebasing.

title: REACH Global discount and quality withhold
questions: What discount applies to Global ACOs in ACO REACH?
How large is the ACO REACH quality withhold?
How do REACH ACOs earn back the quality withhold?
summary: Two reductions are applied to a REACH ACO's benchmark. Global ACOs receive a discount, which was 3 percent in PY2023 and PY2024 and is 4.0 percent in PY2026 per the PY2026 financial operating guide; Professional ACOs have no discount. All ACOs face a quality withhold that can be earned back based on quality performance. In the first two model years (as GPDC) the withhold was 5 percent, with 1 percent tied to performance and 4 percent to reporting; from PY2023 through PY2025 it was 2 percent, all pay-for-performance. For PY2026 CMS raised it back to 5 percent, and the high performers pool, funded by unearned withholds, grows proportionally. In Milliman's example, a 75 percent quality score lowers the benchmark an extra 0.75 percent relative to the old 2 percent withhold.

title: REACH health equity benchmark adjustment (population adjustment)
questions: What is the ACO REACH health equity benchmark adjustment?
How much does the REACH population adjustment add per beneficiary?
What index replaced ADI in REACH for PY2026?
summary: Since PY2023 REACH has adjusted benchmarks per beneficiary to offset historically suppressed spending among underserved populations. CMS scores each aligned beneficiary on area deprivation plus a low-income marker worth 50 points if the person was fully or partially dual eligible or LIS-eligible in the prior 12 months (scores range 1 to 150). In PY2024 the area component averaged national and state Area Deprivation Index ranks; in PY2026 the newly developed Community Deprivation Index, built from 18 census variables, replaces ADI, and the adjustment is called the population adjustment. Each beneficiary-month is adjusted by percentile within the aligned population: plus $30 at or above the 90th percentile, $20 for the 80th-89th, $10 for the 70th-79th, nothing for the 30th-69th, and minus $10 below the 30th percentile. This differs from MSSP's population adjustment, which is an ACO-level benchmark adjustment triggered when at least 15 percent of beneficiaries are LIS or dual.

title: REACH stop-loss reinsurance and risk score caps
questions: What is the optional stop-loss in ACO REACH?
How are REACH stop-loss attachment points set?
What risk score caps apply in ACO REACH for PY2026?
summary: REACH offers optional stop-loss reinsurance to both Global and Professional ACOs to blunt rare high-cost cases. Since PY2023 attachment points are based on expenditure residuals, the gap between a beneficiary's actual spending and a predicted value based on regional spending and risk score, derived from a national reference population. When a residual exceeds the attachment point the excess is paid out, and the ACO pays a per-beneficiary-per-month charge on its benchmark based on baseline experience above the attachment points. On risk scores, REACH caps 2022-to-performance-year growth at 3 percent symmetrically, applies a coding intensity factor (capped at 1 percent for Standard ACOs; raised to 2 percent for High Needs in PY2026), and for PY2026 adds a one-sided 3 percent cap on 2019-to-2026 growth for Standard and New Entrant ACOs and an 8 percent cap for newly voluntarily aligned High Needs beneficiaries. V28 weight reached 100 percent in PY2026 for Standard and New Entrant ACOs.

title: LEAD model: the 2027 successor to ACO REACH
questions: What replaces ACO REACH after 2026?
What is the LEAD model?
How long does the LEAD ACO model run?
summary: CMS announced the Long-term Enhanced ACO Design (LEAD) Model on December 18, 2025 as the successor to ACO REACH, which ends after PY2026. LEAD is a voluntary 10-year model running January 1, 2027 through December 31, 2036. It keeps the two risk options: Global, with up to 100 percent of savings and losses, and Professional, with up to 50 percent. CMS says it will use flexible capitated population-based payments, improved benchmarking and risk adjustment for high-needs patients, and a predictable benchmark path without rebasing, aiming to draw in smaller, independent and rural practices. A Medicaid planning phase runs March 2026 through December 2027, with two states to develop ACO-Medicaid partnerships for dual eligibles, and a CARA initiative supports episode-based arrangements between ACOs and specialists. Detailed financial methodology was not reviewed for this entry; see the cms_models topic for model specifics.

title: Medicare Advantage payment: benchmarks, bids and rebates
questions: How does Medicare pay Medicare Advantage plans?
What is an MA benchmark and how are county quartiles set?
How do MA rebates work?
What happens if an MA plan bids above the benchmark?
summary: Each MA plan submits a bid, the amount it needs to provide Part A and B benefits (including administration and profit) to a standard beneficiary; Part D is bid separately. CMS compares it with a benchmark. Local benchmarks are set by statute at 95, 100, 107.5 or 115 percent of projected county FFS spending, with lower-spending counties getting higher percentages, and are capped at the level that would apply under pre-ACA rules; counties changing quartile get a blend. Benchmarks are raised for plans earning quality bonuses. If a plan bids at or below the benchmark, its base payment is its bid and it also receives a rebate equal to 50, 65 or 70 percent (depending on star rating) of the gap between the risk-adjusted benchmark and the bid, which must fund supplemental benefits, lower cost sharing or lower premiums. If it bids above, it is paid the benchmark and enrollees pay the difference as a premium. Payments are then risk-adjusted with CMS-HCC scores. Regional PPO benchmarks blend FFS rates and plan bids.

title: MA quality bonuses, coding intensity and payments relative to FFS
questions: How much more does Medicare pay for MA enrollees than FFS?
What is the MA quality bonus payment?
What is the MA coding intensity adjustment?
What drives higher Medicare Advantage payments?
summary: By statute, plans awarded quality bonuses get benchmarks 5 percent higher than standard county benchmarks, or 10 percent higher in certain 'double bonus' counties (urban, low-FFS-spending areas with historically high managed care enrollment); unlike most FFS quality programs, these bonuses are not budget neutral. MedPAC estimates that in 2025 Medicare will spend about 20 percent more for MA enrollees than if they were in FFS, roughly $84 billion, out of projected MA payments of $538 billion. MedPAC attributes the gap to coding intensity (MA risk scores about 16 percent above comparable FFS, only partly offset by CMS's 5.9 percent coding adjustment, netting about 10 percent), favorable selection, benchmarks above FFS in low-spending counties, and quality bonuses. MedPAC notes the excess is the main funding source for supplemental benefits. Star ratings methodology is covered in the quality topic.

title: Medical loss ratio (MLR) requirements in MA and Medicaid managed care
questions: What is a medical loss ratio?
What is the minimum MLR for Medicare Advantage plans?
Do Medicaid MCOs have to meet an 85 percent MLR?
What happens if an MA plan's MLR falls below 85 percent?
summary: A medical loss ratio is the share of premium or capitation revenue a plan spends on claims and quality-improving activities rather than administration and profit. For Medicare Advantage, contracts since 2014 must report an MLR; a contract below 0.85 must remit to CMS its total revenue times the shortfall, a contract below 0.85 for three or more consecutive years is barred from new enrollment, and five consecutive years triggers termination. For Medicaid managed care, contracts starting on or after July 1, 2017 must calculate and report an MLR; capitation rates are set to achieve at least 85 percent, any state-mandated minimum must be at least 85 percent, and remittances are owed only if the state requires them. KFF reports 33 states always require remittances and the average Medicaid MCO loss ratio rose from 88 percent in 2023 to 91 percent in 2024. Note that 'MLR' in MSSP means minimum loss rate, a different concept.

title: Medicaid managed care capitation basics
questions: How are Medicaid managed care plans paid?
What share of Medicaid spending goes through MCOs?
What does actuarially sound capitation mean in Medicaid?
summary: States pay Medicaid managed care organizations a fixed per-member, per-month (PMPM) capitation and the MCOs bear the financial risk for covered services. States and their actuaries develop the rates, which must be actuarially sound and are generally set prospectively for a 12-month rating period; CMS reviews and approves them. As of July 2025, 42 states (including DC) used comprehensive risk-based MCOs, contracting with 291 MCOs as of July 2024, and about half of the $919 billion in FY2024 Medicaid spending went to MCO payments. Federal rules cap incentive arrangements in MCO contracts at 105 percent of the approved capitation attributable to the covered enrollees or services. Within this structure, MCOs pay providers through FFS, capitation, or value-based contracts, and states can require value-based purchasing through state directed payments. For providers, Medicaid VBC economics therefore depend on both the state's rates to the MCO and the MCO's contract with the provider.

title: Medicaid state directed payments and value-based purchasing requirements
questions: What are Medicaid state directed payments?
Can states require Medicaid MCOs to use value-based payment?
How did the 2025 reconciliation law change state directed payments?
summary: States generally cannot dictate how MCOs pay providers, but 42 CFR 438.6(c) lets them direct payments in specified ways: requiring value-based purchasing models such as pay-for-performance or bundled payments; requiring participation in multi-payer or Medicaid delivery system reform initiatives; or imposing minimum or maximum fee schedules or uniform rate increases. Most require CMS prior approval via a preprint with an evaluation plan tied to the state quality strategy; since September 10, 2025 preprints lack completeness without minimum quality evaluation elements. The current regulation caps total payment rates for hospital, nursing facility and academic medical center practitioner SDPs at the average commercial rate. Section 71116 of Public Law 119-21 (2025) directs CMS to reduce that limit, with temporary grandfathering; KFF summarizes the new caps as 100 percent of Medicare rates in expansion states and 110 percent in non-expansion states. CMS issued guidance on February 2, 2026 and says final policy will come through rulemaking.

title: HCP-LAN APM Framework categories 1-4
questions: What are the HCP-LAN APM Framework categories?
What is the difference between Category 3A and 3B?
What do Categories 4A, 4B and 4C mean?
Is an upside-only ACO Category 3A or 3B?
summary: The Health Care Payment Learning & Action Network's APM Framework, published in 2016 and refreshed in 2017, classifies payments into four categories. Category 1 is fee-for-service with no link to quality. Category 2 is FFS linked to quality and value: 2A foundational payments for infrastructure and operations, 2B pay-for-reporting, 2C pay-for-performance. Category 3 is APMs built on FFS architecture with cost performance against a target and retrospective reconciliation: 3A shares savings only (upside), 3B adds shared losses (downside); most ACOs fall in 3A or 3B. Category 4 is prospective population-based payment covering a broad set of services: 4A condition-specific (for example a primary care or diabetes population payment), 4B comprehensive, and 4C integrated finance and delivery systems. Models lacking accountability for quality are coded 3N or 4N. The key 3-versus-4 distinction is a single, predominantly prospective payment versus FFS with after-the-fact reconciliation. Procedure-tied episodes stay in Category 3 even if prepaid.

title: How much US health care spending flows through APMs (HCP-LAN measurement and goals)
questions: What share of US health care payments are in alternative payment models?
How common is two-sided risk by line of business?
What are the HCP-LAN 2030 APM goals?
summary: HCP-LAN's 2023 measurement effort, covering the 2022 data year and representing 86.7 percent of the market (64 plans, 4 states and Traditional Medicare), found 24.5 percent of US health care payments flowed through two-sided risk arrangements (Categories 3B and 4). Across all lines of business, 40.6 percent was Category 1, 18.1 percent Category 2, 16.7 percent Category 3A, 15.0 percent 3B and 9.6 percent Category 4 (4A 3.6, 4B 5.3, 4C 0.6). Two-sided risk shares were 16.5 percent in commercial, 38.9 percent in Medicare Advantage, 30.2 percent in Traditional Medicare and 18.7 percent in Medicaid; MA had the most Category 4 (24.6 percent). HCP-LAN's goals for two-sided risk APMs are 25/25/55/50 percent for Medicaid/commercial/MA/Traditional Medicare in 2024, 30/30/65/60 percent in 2025, and 50/50/100/100 percent in 2030. Newer measurement years may exist; re-check before citing.

title: Upside-only vs two-sided risk
questions: What is the difference between upside-only and two-sided risk?
Which MSSP and REACH options are downside risk?
Why do payers push providers to two-sided risk?
summary: In an upside-only (one-sided) arrangement the provider can earn a share of savings against a spending target but owes nothing if spending exceeds it; HCP-LAN classifies this as Category 3A. In a two-sided arrangement the provider also repays a share of losses (Category 3B), and with prospective population-based payment (Category 4) it bears risk directly through capitation. Examples: MSSP BASIC Levels A and B are one-sided with up to 40 percent sharing; Levels C to E and ENHANCED are two-sided with loss caps; ACO REACH Professional shares 50 percent of savings and losses and Global up to 100 percent. Policymakers tie advancement to downside risk because it strengthens incentives: HCP-LAN's goals focus on two-sided risk, CMS's CY 2026 rule shortens MSSP one-sided participation to five years from 2027, and Advanced APM status requires more than nominal financial risk. Two-sided contracts usually add protections such as minimum loss rates, loss caps, risk corridors and stop-loss.

title: Capitation types: PCP capitation, global capitation and PMPM
questions: What is PMPM?
What is the difference between primary care capitation and global capitation?
How does capitation differ from shared savings?
summary: Capitation pays a fixed amount per patient per period, usually per member per month (PMPM), to cover a defined set of services regardless of how many are delivered. Federal MA rules define capitation this way and define global capitation as covering both professional and institutional services (and possibly drugs and supplemental benefits); for MA stop-loss tables, global capitation means all Part A and B services except hospice. Primary care capitation covers only primary care services, so the group keeps FFS for other care, as in ACO REACH's PCC. Total care or global capitation, like REACH's TCC, covers all services and puts the provider at full risk for referrals and facility costs, which triggers stop-loss requirements in MA when referral risk exceeds 25 percent of potential payments. Medicaid MCOs themselves receive PMPM capitation from states. HCP-LAN places capitation with quality accountability in Category 4. Unlike shared savings, which reconciles FFS spending after the fact, capitation moves cash up front. Percent-of-premium capitation (paying a group a share of the plan premium) was not described in the public sources reviewed here.

title: Commercial ACO and shared savings arrangements
questions: How do commercial shared savings contracts work?
How prevalent are APMs in commercial insurance?
How do commercial ACO contracts differ from MSSP?
summary: Commercial payers contract with provider organizations using many of the same building blocks as Medicare: an attributed population, a total-cost-of-care target, quality gates and shared savings (Category 3A) or shared savings and losses (3B), and sometimes capitation (Category 4). Unlike MSSP, terms are privately negotiated and not public, so attribution rules, benchmark trend, minimum savings thresholds, sharing rates, run-out and stop-loss vary by contract. HCP-LAN's 2022-data measurement found commercial lagged other lines in risk: 54.5 percent of commercial payments were pure FFS (Category 1), 30.6 percent Category 2, 10.8 percent Category 3 and 4.1 percent Category 4, with two-sided risk (3B plus 4) at 16.5 percent of payments, against an HCP-LAN goal of 30 percent for 2025 and 50 percent by 2030. HCP-LAN has urged commercial insurers to adopt a consistent national attribution approach led by patient choice of PCP, with claims-based plurality as the fallback.

title: MIPS vs Advanced APMs: QP thresholds, incentive payment and conversion factors
questions: What is a Qualifying APM Participant (QP)?
Is the 5% Advanced APM bonus still paid?
What are the QP thresholds for 2025?
What conversion factor do QPs get in 2026?
summary: Under MACRA's Quality Payment Program, clinicians either participate in MIPS, which adjusts their Medicare payments based on performance, or reach Qualifying APM Participant (QP) status through sufficient participation in Advanced APMs (such as two-sided MSSP tracks), which exempts them from MIPS. QPs historically received a lump-sum APM incentive payment: 5 percent of prior-year professional payments in payment years 2021 through 2024 (per CMS's 2026 notice), 3.5 percent for the 2023 performance year (2025 payment), and 1.88 percent for the 2024 performance year (2026 payment). CMS states that under current law 2026 is the last payment year for these incentives; only Congress can change that. From the 2025 QP performance period, statutory thresholds rose to 75 percent of payments or 50 percent of patients. In place of the bonus, QPs get a 0.75 percent annual fee schedule update versus 0.25 percent for others: CY 2026 conversion factors are $33.57 for QPs and $33.40 for non-QPs, both including a one-year 2.5 percent statutory increase. Partial QPs may opt into MIPS.

title: Risk corridors, stop-loss and reinsurance in VBC contracts
questions: What is a risk corridor?
What is the difference between a risk corridor and stop-loss?
How do VBC contracts protect providers from catastrophic claims?
summary: Risk corridors divide savings or losses into bands measured as a percent of the benchmark and give the provider a declining share in each band, limiting exposure to extreme results while preserving incentives near the target. ACO REACH is the clearest public example: Professional ACOs keep 50 percent of results within 5 percent of benchmark and progressively less beyond; Global ACOs keep 100 percent within the first band (25 percent of benchmark through PY2025, 10 percent in PY2026). Stop-loss, or reinsurance, instead protects against individual high-cost patients: costs above an attachment point or deductible are partly covered in exchange for a premium or charge. REACH offers optional stop-loss based on residuals above predicted spending; MA physician incentive plan rules require stop-loss covering 90 percent of referral costs above set thresholds for groups at substantial financial risk. MSSP uses neither formal corridors nor stop-loss, relying instead on minimum savings/loss rates, sharing rates, loss caps and truncation of extreme per-beneficiary spending in benchmark calculations.
